## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Technical Foundations: LoRA, QLoRA, and PEFT

**Why fine-tuning matters.** Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained general-purpose LLM to specific tasks (domain specialization, safety alignment, task accuracy) at far lower cost than training from scratch. It is "the difference between giving a chef a special recipe and retraining the entire culinary school" [9]. Fine-tuning is preferable to in-context learning or zero/few-shot inference when you need specificity, accuracy, customized interactions, data privacy, and handling of rare scenarios [11]. A practical rule of thumb: "reach for RAG when the problem is 'the model doesn't know this fact,' and reach for LoRA or QLoRA when the problem is 'the model doesn't behave the way I need'" [35].

**LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation).** LoRA freezes the original model weights and trains only smaller "low-rank" matrices (A and B with rank r), which are then merged back into the original model. This reduces time, memory, and cost [3]. The LoRA paper states this method can minimize trainable parameters by up to 10,000 times and GPU memory necessity by 3 times while performing on par or better than full fine-tuning on various tasks [1]. LoRA exploits the observation that weight updates for adaptation are approximately low-rank: instead of updating the full weight matrix W, it freezes W and injects two small matrices A and B such that W′ = W + BA, where BA is low-rank (small r). Only A and B are trained [9]. Typical LoRA ranks: r ∈ [4, 64]; start small (r=8). Learning rate is often higher than full fine-tuning (1e-4 → 1e-3) [9]. Key hyperparameters: rank (r, typically 8-256) and alpha (α, typically 2×r). LoRA is applied to attention layers (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj) and MLP layers (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj) [34]. LoRA adapters are small (6MB-8MB) and can be paired with base models, enabling multi-tenancy [8].

**QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation).** QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization with LoRA, dramatically reducing memory requirements [7]. It works by backpropagating gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA) [4][5]. QLoRA introduces three key innovations [1][2][4][5]:
- **(a) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)**: an information-theoretically optimal quantization data type for normally distributed weights that yields better empirical results than 4-bit Integers and 4-bit Floats.
- **(b) Double Quantization**: quantizes the quantization constants themselves, saving an average of about 0.37 bits per parameter (approximately 3 GB for a 65B model). For a blocksize of 64, this reduces memory footprint per parameter from 32/64 = 0.5 bits to 8/64 + 32/(64·256) = 0.127 bits, a reduction of 0.373 bits per parameter [1].
- **(c) Paged Optimizers**: use NVIDIA unified memory to avoid gradient checkpointing memory spikes that occur when processing a mini-batch with a long sequence length [1][2].

**Key QLoRA results.** The best model family, Guanaco, outperformed all previously openly released models on the Vicuna benchmark, reaching 99.3% of ChatGPT's performance level while requiring only 24 hours of fine-tuning on a single GPU [2][4][5]. QLoRA enables fine-tuning a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance [4][5]. The authors fine-tuned over 1,000 models across 8 instruction datasets, multiple model types (LLaMA, T5), and scales up to 65B parameters. Key findings: QLoRA fine-tuning on small high-quality datasets achieves state-of-the-art results even with smaller models than previous SoTA; GPT-4 evaluations serve as a cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation; and current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy for accurately evaluating chatbot performance [5]. Known limitations include slow 4-bit inference, potential instability with fp16 compute type, and issues with resuming LoRA training [4].

**Memory savings with QLoRA.** A 7B model drops from ~28GB (full fine-tuning) to ~6GB with QLoRA; a 13B model from ~52GB to ~10GB; and a 70B model from ~280GB to ~48GB [7]. QLoRA can reduce memory footprint by up to 4 times versus LoRA [3]. QLoRA uses significantly less storage than LoRA, making it the better choice when storage or resources are limited [3]. QLoRA requires more LoRA adapters (applied to all linear layers) but achieves performance comparable to full finetuning [8].

**PEFT library performance figures.** On an A100 80GB GPU, fully fine-tuning bigscience/T0_3B requires 47.14GB GPU memory, while PEFT-LoRA uses 14.4GB and PEFT-LoRA with DeepSpeed CPU offloading uses 9.8GB. For the 12B-parameter bigscience/mt0-xxl, full fine-tuning runs out of memory, but LoRA fits in 56GB and offloading reduces this to 22GB. PEFT-LoRA achieved 0.863 accuracy on the raft twitter_complaints dataset, close to the human baseline of 0.897 and Flan-T5's 0.892, with a final checkpoint of only 19MB compared to 11GB for the full model. For Stable Diffusion v1-4, LoRA reduces training memory from 27.5GB to 15.5GB, and further to 8.12GB with gradient checkpointing, with a final checkpoint size of just 8.8MB [10]. PEFT supports quantization, helps avoid catastrophic forgetting, and enables training and inference of very large models on consumer hardware [10].

**LoRA variants.** QA LoRA (quantization-aware, for diffusion models), LongLoRA (uses shift short attention for longer contexts), AdaLoRA (dynamically allocates rank based on layer importance via SVD), and DoRA (decomposes into single-rank components with pruning, enabled via use_dora=True in LoraConfig) [8]. Modern quantization strategies include AWQ (activation-aware weight quantization, preserving salient weights, enabling 3x speedup on LLaMA-2 70B), AffineQuant (affine transformations for better PTQ, achieving C4 perplexity 15.76 on LLaMA2-7B with W4A4), and Unsloth's Dynamic 4-bit Quantization (built on BitsandBytes, uses <10% more VRAM while improving accuracy, e.g., compressing Llama 3.2 Vision 11B from 20GB to 6.5GB) [8].

**Quantization methods.** PTQ (post-training quantization) is simpler but may degrade accuracy; GPTQ is layer-wise, second-order-aware quantization that preserves accuracy at 4-bit; AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) accounts for activation distributions and often outperforms GPTQ at 4-bit [9].

**Fine-tuning workflow.** (1) Pick a base model (capability vs. cost trade-off); (2) Choose a method (full fine-tune, instruction FT, PEFT/LoRA, or RLHF); (3) Prepare data (instruction-response pairs); (4) Train (using Trainer, Accelerate, or custom loops); (5) Evaluate & iterate (automatic metrics + human evaluation); (6) Deploy (serve frozen base + adapters or merged weights) [9]. Google Cloud's 4-step process: data preparation (collect, clean, format, split into train/validation/test), choosing an approach (full vs. PEFT), training (set hyperparameters, monitor with validation set), evaluation and deployment [16].

**Fine-tuning types.** Supervised fine-tuning (labeled datasets; text classification, NER, sentiment analysis), instruction fine-tuning (instructions and responses; chatbots, QA systems, code generation), few-shot learning (few examples in prompt), transfer learning, domain-specific fine-tuning (legal, medical, financial), multi-task learning (requiring 50,000–100,000 examples), and sequential fine-tuning [16][11].

**Best practices.** Use clear instruction-response pairs (system + user + assistant format) [9]. Use both automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/EM/Perplexity) and human judgment [9]. Keep base model frozen + load LoRA adapters at runtime for memory-efficient deployment [9]. Data quality is paramount: "ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and free of errors or biases" [16]. "Quality matters more than volume: 500 carefully written, consistent examples usually beat 5,000 scraped, noisy ones" [35]. FAQs advise starting with a few hundred high-quality examples [13]. Prevent catastrophic forgetting with smaller learning rates, fewer epochs, mixed data, and adapters [13]. Common pitfalls: setting learning rate too high, targeting only q_proj and v_proj, using too-small or repetitive datasets, leaving the pad token unset, skipping an evaluation split, and merging directly from a 4-bit model [35].

**Limitations of fine-tuning.** PEFT may not capture tasks requiring major internal reconfiguration; quantization can degrade performance; SFT/PEFT alone doesn't ensure safety (RLHF or human-in-loop needed for high-stakes outputs) [9]. Fine-tuning does not prevent hallucination "as this is an inherent problem of LLMs"; it can help restrict to domain knowledge but at the cost of general knowledge [18]. Injecting knowledge via fine-tuning is very difficult: LLaMA was pretrained on 1.4 trillion tokens, so fine-tuning on even 1 billion tokens (less than 0.1% of pretraining data) cannot meaningfully inject new knowledge — fine-tuning primarily teaches format (e.g., QA structure) rather than deep knowledge [12]. A model fine-tuned on noisy, inconsistent, or poorly formatted data will perform worse than the base model on the target task — a phenomenon sometimes called "fine-tuning degradation" [29].

**Fine-tuning vs. RAG.** Fine-tuning alters the model's parameters, offering improved accuracy, enhanced specificity, reduced hallucinations, customized interactions, cost-effectiveness, and reduced bias, but carries risks of catastrophic forgetting, higher resource costs, stronger data demands, and overfitting. RAG augments prompts with external knowledge, providing dynamic knowledge integration and contextual relevance, but has limited accuracy and complexity in maintenance [16]. For strictly restricting answers to a new dataset, combine fine-tuning with RAG rather than relying on fine-tuning alone [14].

### 2. Compute Requirements Across Price Ranges

**VRAM rule of thumb.** Full fine-tuning requires roughly 16 GB of GPU VRAM per 1 billion model parameters (e.g., ~208 GB for a 13B model) [26][28]. This is significantly higher than the 2GB per 1B parameters needed for inference due to additional memory for optimizer states, gradients, and training data [28]. Training VRAM consists of four components: model weights (BF16 = 2 bytes/param; 4-bit NF4 = 0.5 bytes/param), gradients (same precision as trainable weights), optimizer states (AdamW stores two FP32 moments per trainable param, i.e., 8 bytes/param), and activations (roughly 2–20 GB at batch size 1, sequence length 512) [27].

- 7B/8B models: ~88 GB for full FT, ~20 GB for LoRA, ~8 GB for QLoRA

### 3. Project Ideas with Novel Angles

#### Project Idea A: Personal Writing-Style Clone / "Twin" LLM

**Novel angle / personal twist.** Fine-tune an LLM to mimic your own writing or speaking style using your personal data (exported chat logs, journal entries, emails, or academic papers). This is inherently personal and original — no two people have the same data. Watson Chua, a Staff Data Scientist at GovTech, did exactly this: he exported WhatsApp conversations with his wife and nine friends as training data, combined consecutive messages within five minutes, grouped chats into conversation blocks (split if over 3000 tokens), and formatted them using Llama3's prompt template into a JSONL file, yielding 4,845 training lines. He chose Mistral-7B-v0.2 as the base model (rather than an instruction-tuned version) to avoid prompt template conflicts, and used QLoRA for memory efficiency. Training parameters: max_length=3000, lora_r=32, lora_alpha=64, lora_dropout=0.05, epochs=5, batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=8. He hosted the model on a T4 GPU (16GB) at $0.40/hour, wrapped it in a FastAPI service, and built a Telegram bot using python-telegram-bot. User testing showed good results with his wife, mixed results with friends, and one hallucination incident. Suggested improvements: down-sampling wife-heavy data, creating separate user roles (wife, friend, boss), adding background information via completion fine-tuning, using better serving tools like vLLM, and reducing hosting costs. Code available at github.com/watsonchua/finetune-your-clone [38].

**Alternative data source — academic papers.** V. Iosifidis's blog series explains how to fine-tune an LLM with your own data to mimic your writing style using academic research papers as the data source. Key principles: prioritize quality over quantity (e.g., 1,000 high-quality samples vs. 10,000 low-quality ones); clean text by removing duplicates, formatting errors, and special characters; use the 'scipdf' parser with GROBID; filter out paragraphs shorter than 500 characters; retain metadata (e.g., section names); ~500 samples is workable. For dataset generation, use back-translation with an ensemble of open-source LLMs (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Configurable-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Falcon3-10B-Instruct-GPTQ-Int4) to create instruction-answer triples (instruction, rejected, accepted). A carefully designed prompt with 2-shot examples and a 'tip' (offering $200) improves output quality and JSON formatting. Filter out bad samples using keyword rules and length constraints (100–650 characters). Store final training data in JSON format with user/assistant roles [37].

**Required skills.** Data extraction and cleaning (WhatsApp export, PDF parsing with PyMuPDF/scipdf/GROBID), data preprocessing (chunking, deduplication, formatting into chat templates), QLoRA fine-tuning with Hugging Face TRL/PEFT, basic deployment (FastAPI, Telegram bot, or Ollama) [38][37].

**Dataset sources.** Personal data exports (WhatsApp, Telegram, email, journal entries, academic papers) — inherently unique and personal [38][37]. For a non-personal variant, the dvgodoy/yoda_sentences dataset (720 English-to-Yoda sentence pairs) demonstrates the same style-transfer concept with a public dataset [33].

**Compute.** Free/Colab: feasible for small models (e.g., Phi-3 Mini 3.8B on 6GB GTX 1060 in ~35 minutes [33]). Paid: Watson Chua's run cost ~$60 on A10G-Small at $1/hour for ~60 hours [38]. A 7B QLoRA run on a 24GB GPU (RTX 3090/4090) at ~$0.5–1.0/hour is the sweet spot [26].

**Interview stand-out.** Demonstrates the full pipeline from private data collection → preprocessing → PEFT fine-tuning → deployment (Telegram bot/API). Shows judgment about data privacy (not publicly releasing the bot), and the ability to evaluate subjective quality (user testing with real people). The "clone" angle is memorable and demonstrates understanding that fine-tuning changes behavior/style, not just knowledge [38][35].

#### Project Idea B: Domain-Specific Instruction-Tuned Assistant via Synthetic Data Generation

**Novel angle / personal twist.** Pick a niche domain you genuinely know (e.g., a specific software tool, a hobby, a sport, a game) and build an instruction-tuned assistant using a two-stage pipeline: (1) extract domain text from official documentation/PDFs, (2) use a larger LLM to synthetically generate high-quality instruction-response pairs, (3) fine-tune a small open model with QLoRA. Nicholas Renotte's tutorial demonstrates this exactly: he fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B to teach it about IBM Cognos TM1 (financial planning software). He used Docling for document processing (hybrid chunking and contextualization), converted a TM1 PDF documentation into chunks, used Qwen 2.5 14B via LightLLM to generate instruction-tuning pairs, trained on a RunPod RTX A5000 (25GB VRAM), and deployed locally with Ollama. Key improvements that worked: increasing rank to 256 and alpha to 512 (following Sebastian Raschka's recommendation of alpha being double the rank); increasing epochs to 100; removing context from instruction pairs; and implementing a data quality filter that uses an LLM to classify each instruction pair on accuracy and style (1-10 scale), keeping only pairs scoring 6+ in both categories (reducing dataset from 2006 to 1078 lines). Final training achieved loss 0.55 and mean token accuracy 0.95. The entire workflow can be adapted to any custom dataset by swapping the PDF and adjusting the Docling chunking. Code at github.com/nicknochnack/EndTo... [36].

**Required skills.** Document processing (Docling/PyMuPDF), synthetic data generation with LLM APIs, data quality filtering, QLoRA fine-tuning with TRL SFTTrainer, local deployment with Ollama [36].

**Dataset sources.** Official product documentation PDFs (any domain), or public domain corpora. For a first project, the Sunny Savita tutorial demonstrates non-instruction fine-tuning on a pharma-domain PDF (metformin) using PyMuPDF (fitz) for text extraction, cleaning and chunking data, converting to Hugging Face Dataset format with a 'text' column, tokenization (truncation/padding to 512 tokens, assigning input_ids as labels for causal LM), and loading TinyLlama 1.1B as the base model. Full fine-tuning fails with OOM, so QLoRA is the solution: load model in 8-bit (bitsandbytes), apply LoRA config (task type CAUSAL_LM, r=rank, lora_alpha, target modules q_proj and v_proj, lora_dropout 0.05), train with TrainingArguments and Trainer. Training completes with loss 9.66 over 2 epochs. Example datasets for each fine-tuning type: non-instructional (FineWeb, pile pubmed abstract, OpenWebText), instruction (mental health counseling, Alpaca, OpenOrca), preference alignment (Anthropic, UltraFeedback with 'chosen' and 'rejected' columns) [20].

**Compute.** Free/Colab: TinyLlama 1.1B QLoRA works on Colab [20]. Paid: RunPod RTX A5000 (25GB) for the Renotte workflow [36]. A 7B model QLoRA needs ~8GB VRAM [27]; a 3B-8B model with a few thousand examples takes 30 minutes to a few hours [35].

**Interview stand-out.** Shows the modern synthetic-data-generation workflow that industry uses; demonstrates data quality filtering (an advanced skill); shows deployment via Ollama; the domain can be chosen to align with the target company's products. The baseline-vs-fine-tuned comparison (hallucination reduction) is a compelling narrative [36].

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. The RAG Landscape and Why It Matters for Big Tech Careers

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is described as "the most important AI architecture pattern of 2025–2026. It powers enterprise AI assistants at Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and thousands of startups" [2]. RAG is fundamentally "like giving your AI a memory upgrade *and* a Google search bar. Instead of making up answers based on what it 'thinks' it learned during training, your model can now fetch real-time, relevant info — basically, it stopped hallucinating and started citing sources" [1].

The core RAG concept: RAG solves LLM hallucination and knowledge cutoff problems by adding a memory layer — documents are chunked and embedded into a vector database, relevant chunks are retrieved on query, and passed as context to the LLM for grounded answers [2]. The standard RAG architecture pipeline is: User query → query embedding → vector database similarity search → top-K chunk retrieval → context + query to LLM → grounded answer with citations [2].

RAG combines retrieval-based and generation-based models, allowing language models like GPT to access external knowledge sources and produce more accurate, contextually relevant outputs. The key idea is to integrate a retriever module into a generative model, such as a transformer-based language model like GPT, to improve its ability to generate more informative, accurate, and contextually relevant responses [3].

**Key interview insight**: "RAG systems are fundamentally data pipelines with multiple failure modes. A system that works for 10,000 documents will collapse at 10 million without careful architecture choices around caching, distributed indexing, and graceful degradation. The best candidates don't just know HNSW from IVF indexing, they can explain when each choice will break under production load and how to recover gracefully. Chunking is not a preprocessing step you can ignore, it's a core architectural decision that determines what information your RAG system can and cannot access. The biggest mistake is treating RAG as a simple 'embed, store, retrieve' pipeline without addressing failure modes. You should always discuss how you would measure and iterate on retrieval precision, answer faithfulness, and end-to-end system performance" [8].

### 4. Advanced RAG Techniques

#### 4.1 Agentic Hybrid Search

The core argument from The New Stack: most RAG systems fail not because of the LLM or embeddings, but because they rely solely on semantic similarity for retrieval, which often pulls in contextually irrelevant documents for nuanced queries. The proposed solution combines hybrid search backed by structured metadata with LLM-driven decision-making. Instead of the naive flow of "question → search → generate," agentic hybrid search follows "question → analyze → search(s) → generate." The LLM analyzes each query to decide which knowledge base to query, what metadata filters to apply, and whether to run multiple targeted searches. This enables querying multiple knowledge bases, crafting tailored search queries, applying metadata filters (e.g., card name, bank name, policy section, dates), and decomposing complex questions into sub-searches [6].

Benefits: improved accuracy, enhanced user trust, broader use cases, simplified maintenance, and future-proof scalability. Tradeoffs: increased latency, higher inference costs, and added orchestration complexity, though these can be mitigated with caching or limiting analysis to complex queries [6].

From Towards AI: Traditional RAG relies solely on vector similarity for retrieving relevant document chunks, which works well for semantic matching but fails when users input specific keywords, IDs, or exact terms. The solution is hybrid search, which combines keyword search (e.g., BM25) with vector similarity to improve retrieval accuracy [9].

#### 4.2 Reference Architecture for Agentic Hybrid Retrieval (arXiv paper)

An arXiv paper (2604.16394v1, cs.IR, March 2026) by Riccardo Terrenzi and colleagues from the University of Southern Denmark proposes a reference architecture for agentic hybrid retrieval in dataset search. Key elements [7]:
- Combines BM25 lexical search with dense-embedding retrieval via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), orchestrated by an LLM agent that iteratively plans queries, evaluates result sufficiency, and reranks candidates in a Plan–Retrieve–Evaluate loop
- Introduces an offline metadata augmentation step where an LLM generates 5–10 pseudo-queries per dataset record, indexed alongside or instead of original metadata (to address vocabulary mismatch between user intent and provider-authored metadata)
- Two architectural styles examined: a single ReAct-style agent and a multi-agent horizontal architecture with four specialized agents (Planner, Retriever, Evaluator, Reranker) communicating via typed JSON contracts under feedback control
- Analyzes quality-attribute tradeoffs (modifiability, observability, performance, governance, failure isolation, operational complexity)
- Defines a seven-variant ablation framework (V1–V7) to isolate contributions of BM25, dense retrieval, RRF, agentic control, pseudo-queries, and multi-agent decomposition
- Evaluation metrics include nDCG, MAP, Recall, and MRR, plus architectural metrics like iterations per query, token consumption, stability across runs, and schema validation failure rate
- Planned benchmarks include ACORDAR 2.0, NTCIR-15 Data Search, and TARGET
- Emphasizes governance through iteration budgets, provenance traces, versioned artifacts, and audit safeguards for LLM nondeterminism

#### 4.3 Context Engineering and Hybrid Search (Elastic)

From Elastic Search Labs: search has shifted from human-driven text-box queries to AI agents automatically retrieving and compiling answers — search is now performed invisibly through tools. To make agentic AI reliable, the context supplied to LLMs must be engineered to reflect subjective relevance and ground truth. Key capabilities [10]:
- **Aggregations and non-content signals**: Aggregations provide numerical facts about retrieved data, help manage context window size (e.g., reducing 100k documents to a few hundred tokens), and can be hierarchically nested. Non-content signals — popularity, freshness, geo-location, categories, host diversity, price bands — help agents weigh the importance of context. Examples include boosting recent/popular articles, adjusting e-commerce results by sales and stock, and prioritizing high-severity bug tracker issues.
- **Security enforcement**: Elastic's built-in security framework ensures agents only receive authorized data. Supports fine-grained permissions, role-based access control (RBAC), attribute-based access control (ABAC), document-level security (DLS), field-level security (FLS), and integration with enterprise identity systems (LDAP, SAML, OIDC).
- **Agent Builder**: A Kibana-based chat interface for creating and managing agents and tools, with built-in MCP/A2A servers, programmatic APIs, and pre-built system tools. Supports ES|QL query generation from natural language. Hybrid search in ES|QL is achieved via the `semantic_text` field type and `FORK`/`FUSE` commands (with FUSE using reciprocal rank fusion by default).
- **Search templates**: Allow predefined query structures for external agentic tools, standardizing boilerplate code, controlling inputs/outputs, and enabling faster iteration on search logic.
- **Unified memory**: Elastic naturally serves as long-term memory for agentic AI due to its distributed, near-real-time search platform, while Agent Builder manages short-term memory and chat history.

#### 4.4 GraphRAG

GraphRAG is defined as "a specialized subclass of the RAG framework" that "utilizes graph structures to systematically organize and retrieve domain-specific knowledge." Its workflow encompasses two key stages: offline indexing and online retrieval. GraphRAG addresses limitations of standard RAG by using graph structures to organize and retrieve domain-specific knowledge [19].

From Neo4j: "A vector database is like a 'semantic search engine' — great at finding passages that sound similar to your question, but not always great at showing how things are connected. A knowledge graph, by contrast, is like a semantic map: it doesn't just tell you what's relevant, it shows you how concepts, entities, and data points relate to one another. GraphRAG addresses these limitations by incorporating structured domain knowledge." Vector-only RAG struggles with aggregation, explainability, and fine-grained control, while knowledge graphs provide structured queries (Cypher), combine structured and unstructured data, and offer explainable paths. A key limitation of vector search demonstrated in the tutorial: it returns 4 open tickets when there are actually 5 — Cypher solves aggregation problems. #### 4.5 Multimodal RAG

Multimodal RAG extends traditional text-only RAG systems to handle images, audio, video, and text simultaneously. It creates unified vector spaces where all data types are converted into embeddings, enabling "any-to-any" retrieval — for example, a voice query can retrieve a diagram, or a photo can surface a relevant manual paragraph. The pipeline consists of five stages: (1) embedding inputs using multimodal models like CLIP or LLaVA, (2) storing embeddings in a vector database (Meilisearch, FAISS, Milvus, or Pinecone), (3) retrieving similar items by comparing query vectors, (4) fusing information across modalities using cross-modal attention mechanisms, and (5) generating responses with an LLM using the fused context. Real-world applications include customer support (analyzing screenshots, voice messages, and documentation together) and healthcare (combining X-rays, doctor's notes, and spoken symptoms) [30].

**MegaRAG** (arXiv 2512.20626v2, Apr 20 2026) is a multimodal knowledge graph-based RAG system that automatically constructs multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) from visually rich documents using multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Authors are from National Taiwan University, E.SUN Financial Holding, and National Kaohsiung Normal University. It addresses a key limitation of existing KG-based RAG methods like GraphRAG and LightRAG, which are text-only and fail to leverage visual cues such as figures, tables, and page layouts [27].

MegaRAG methodology: Builds an MMKG in two stages. First, an MLLM (GPT-4o-mini) extracts page-level entities and relations in parallel from text, figures, tables, and full-page images, then merges them into an initial graph. Second, a refinement stage retrieves page-specific subgraphs and prompts the MLLM to add missing cross-modal and cross-page relations. Entities, relations, and page images are embedded using GME-Qwen2-VL-2B in a unified vector space. Retrieval uses dual-level keywords (low-level and high-level). To reduce modality bias, MegaRAG uses a two-stage generation process: first generates separate intermediate answers from the retrieved knowledge graph and from page images, then fuses them into a final answer [27].

Key results: On textual global QA, MegaRAG achieved average win rates of 59.0% for Comprehensiveness, 71.4% for Diversity, 74.8% for Empowerment, and 71.8% Overall against baselines. On multimodal global QA, it achieved average win rates of 83.3%, 92.7%, 84.7%, and 89.5% respectively. On local QA, MegaRAG reached 64.85% accuracy on SlideVQA (2k), more than double the strongest baseline, and outperformed baselines on all RealMMBench subsets, including 58.37% on FinSlides and 60.86% on TechSlides. Code available at https://github.com/AI-Application-and-Integration-Lab/MegaRAG. Limitations include single-document scope, coarse figure-level entity representation, and potential hallucination propagation from MLLM-based graph construction [27].

### 5. RAG Evaluation (The Critical Differentiator)

#### 5.1 Core Metrics and the "RAG Triad"

RAG systems combine a Retriever and a Generator, each with distinct failure modes. Retriever failures include low precision (noise), low recall (missing information), and poor ranking. Generator failures include hallucination/lack of faithfulness, poor synthesis, and irrelevance to query. The industry has converged on the "RAG Triad" of core metrics, typically implemented via LLM-as-a-judge [11]:
1. **Context Relevance** (query↔retrieved context, enterprise target >70%)
2. **Faithfulness/Groundedness** (context↔response, target >90%)
3. **Answer Relevance** (query↔response, target >85%)

From Atlan, the standard framework evaluates RAG across two dimensions — retrieval quality and generation quality — using four core metrics: (1) Faithfulness (does the answer reflect retrieved content without unsupported claims), (2) Answer relevance (does the answer address the question), (3) Context precision (are retrieved chunks ranked with most relevant first), and (4) Context recall (does retrieved context contain everything needed) [12].

From Patronus AI: The five key metrics are context relevance, context sufficiency, answer relevance, answer correctness, and answer hallucination. Traditional statistical metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and perplexity are inadequate for LLM evaluation because they rely on exact word matches; instead, embedding-based similarity and LLM-as-a-judge approaches (including specialized judge models like Lynx and Glider) are recommended [15].

From Vectara: RAGAs provides two main capabilities: RAG metrics evaluation and synthetic data generation for creating question/answer pairs. Four key metrics: faithfulness (factual consistency against retrieved context), answer similarity (semantic resemblance to ground truth), answer relevancy (pertinence to the question), and answer correctness (weighted combination of factual consistency and semantic similarity). Vectara's HHEM (Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model) is a classification model that is more reliable and robust than LLM-as-a-judge faithfulness approaches [14].

#### 5.4 The "Context Trustworthiness" Gap (Fifth Dimension)

From Atlan: Traditional RAG evaluation measures pipeline performance but assumes the retrieval index itself is trustworthy, which can lead to confident but wrong business answers when content is stale, unowned, or misaligned with canonical sources. A concrete example shows a RAG system scoring 0.95 faithfulness, 1.0 relevance, precision, and recall, yet returning a wrong answer because the glossary definition of "monthly active users" was eight months old and excluded trial users per a recent redefinition. Context trustworthiness asks four questions about every piece of content in the retrieval index: Freshness (when last reviewed), Ownership (is there an accountable owner), Lineage integrity (can it be traced to canonical source), and Canonical alignment (is it consistent with authoritative definitions) [12].

Three best practices recommended: (1) Use trusted dashboards (Tableau, Power BI, Looker) as ground truth — if an agent disagrees with a dashboard, the dashboard is right, and the disagreement signals index gaps; (2) Treat every user correction as an evaluation signal and route it back to the retrieval index; (3) Monitor index health continuously, tracking definition age, ownership coverage, lineage completeness, and schema version currency [12].

As Siva Shanmugam, Executive Product Leader at Salesforce puts it: "evaluation helps you determine whether the answer is factually correct, and whether the information is supported by the retrieved documents" [12].

#### 5.5 Recommended Evaluation Strategy

A three-phase evaluation strategy is recommended [11]:
1. **Development & CI/CD** using RAGAs/DeepEval with golden datasets and synthetic data generation
2. **Pre-Production benchmarking** against RAGBench/CRAG for stress-testing robustness
3. **Production observability** using OpenTelemetry instrumentation with Langfuse/Arize Phoenix/LangSmith, capturing user feedback and closing the loop by adding real-world failures back to the CI/CD test suite

Future trends: agentic RAG evaluation (assessing reasoning processes and tool selection), multi-modal RAG metrics, the rise of specialized open-source evaluator models, and continued standardization/interoperability across the LLMOps ecosystem [11].

Tracing and observability: OpenTelemetry (OTEL) has emerged as the vendor-neutral standard, with core concepts of Traces, Spans, and Attributes. The GenAI semantic conventions (semconv.ai) standardize attribute names for LLM calls, retrieval operations, and tool usage. This standardization decouples applications from observability platforms, preventing vendor lock-in [11].

### 1. Multimodal LLM Landscape and Architecture

**Standard VLM architecture.** A Future AGI visual guide (May 2026) explains that multimodal LLMs share a core architectural pattern: (1) encode each non-text modality with a domain-specific encoder, (2) project the encoder's features into the language model's token space, and (3) decode with a text-only LLM that sees both projected tokens and the user's text prompt. The vision-language variant has three components: a vision encoder (e.g., CLIP ViT-L/14, SigLIP, InternViT-6B, Pixtral-ViT) that converts images into patch embeddings; a connector that maps visual features into the LLM's token space; and a text-only autoregressive decoder (e.g., Llama 3/4, Qwen2/3, Mistral). Three dominant fusion strategies exist: projection-based connectors (LLaVA, NVLM, Pixtral) which map each patch to a token; Q-Former (BLIP-2) which compresses patches into fewer query tokens; and cross-attention adapter layers (Flamingo, OpenFlamingo) inserted into a frozen LLM. Reference architectures covered include LLaVA-NeXT, NVIDIA NVLM 1.0, Mistral Pixtral Large, BLIP-2, and OpenFlamingo. A benchmark snapshot (May 2026) shows Pixtral Large leading on DocVQA (~90%), ChartQA (~88%), and MathVista (~85%), while NVLM 1.0 leads on MMMU (~78%) and OCRBench (~92%). ## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. General Transformer Background

The transformer is a family of artificial neural network architectures based on multi-head attention, introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Google researchers. Unlike RNNs (e.g., LSTM), transformers process tokens in parallel, making them more efficient for training on large datasets. They are the foundation of LLMs like GPT, BERT, and T5, and are applied across NLP, computer vision, audio, robotics, and more. The original transformer required learning rate warmup for convergence; a 2020 paper found that pre-LN normalization (layer norm before sublayers) stabilizes training without warmup. Core components include tokenizers (BPE, unigram), embedding layers, transformer layers (encoder/decoder), and un-embedding layers. Positional encodings (sinusoidal) inject token order information. Subsequent developments include alternative activations (GELU, SwiGLU), normalizations (RMSNorm), positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi), efficient implementations (FlashAttention, KV caching, quantization, speculative decoding), and sub-quadratic transformers (Reformer, sparse attention). Transformers have been adapted for multimodality: vision transformers, speech recognition (Whisper), and image/video generation (DALL-E, Parti, Muse, Phenaki). Applications include machine translation, summarization, code generation, NER, speech-to-text, biological sequence analysis, protein folding (AlphaFold), and chess evaluation (grandmaster-level Elo 2895) [1].

### 2. Time Series Forecasting Transformers

#### 2.1 Informer (AAAI 2021 Best Paper)

The Informer paper ("Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting," AAAI-21) identifies three critical limitations of the vanilla Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting (LSTF): (1) quadratic time complexity O(L²) and memory usage of self-attention, (2) memory bottlenecks when stacking layers for long inputs, and (3) slow step-by-step dynamic decoding for long outputs. Informer has three distinctive characteristics:
- **ProbSparse self-attention**: reduces time and memory complexity to O(L log L) by identifying dominant query-key pairs via a sparsity measurement (max-mean approximation of KL divergence).
- **Self-attention distilling**: uses Conv1d, ELU activation, and max-pooling to halve cascading layer inputs, reducing total space complexity to O((2−ϵ)L log L) and enabling processing of extremely long inputs.
- **Generative-style decoder**: predicts long sequences in a single forward pass using start tokens and masked attention, avoiding cumulative error propagation.

Experiments were conducted on four large-scale datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1 for electricity transformer temperature, ECL for electricity consumption, and Weather). Informer significantly outperformed baselines including LSTMa, LSTnet, DeepAR, ARIMA, Prophet, LogTrans, and Reformer. In univariate forecasting, Informer achieved MSE reductions of 26.8% (at horizon 168), 52.4% (at 336), and 60.1% (at 720) over LSTMa, and average decreases of 49.3%, 61.1%, and 65.1% over DeepAR/ARIMA/Prophet. In multivariate forecasting, MSE decreased by 26.6% (at 168), 28.2% (at 336), and 34.3% (at 720) on average. Ablation studies confirm ProbSparse attention avoids out-of-memory failures in extreme long-input cases, self-attention distilling enables processing inputs beyond 720 length, and the generative decoder maintains stable performance with prediction offsets while dynamic decoding fails. Source code and the ETT dataset are publicly available on GitHub [2].

#### 2.2 PatchTST (ICLR 2023)

PatchTST (Patch Time Series Transformer, "A Time Series is Worth 64 Words," ICLR 2023) is a Transformer-based framework for time-series forecasting, classification, and representation learning. Its core design splits each univariate series into patch tokens, linearly projects them into embeddings, and processes all channels independently with a shared Transformer encoder. This channel-independent patching preserves local temporal semantics, reduces self-attention complexity, and enables longer look-back windows. Training supports supervised MSE forecasting and self-supervised masked patch reconstruction, with regularization including dropout, label smoothing, stochastic depth, gradient clipping, and test-matched augmentation.

Empirically, PatchTST outperforms models such as Informer, FEDformer, Autoformer, DLinear, LSTM, and TCN across multiple benchmarks: up to 21% lower MSE on long-horizon datasets, 92.59% accuracy on UCI-HAR classification, 24–59% RMSE reductions in heart-rate prediction, ~80% error reduction in monsoon rainfall forecasting, and order-of-magnitude MSE improvements on financial data when combined with VMD+ASWL. Known limitations include blindness to cross-channel dependencies, under-representation of high-frequency content, and task-dependent patch design trade-offs. The model is computationally efficient, processing 10,000 windows in 14–21 seconds on GPUs and training in minutes per epoch. Extensions include CT-PatchTST (inter-channel dependencies), Hi-WaveTST (high-frequency wavelet features), and QKCV attention (static categorical context) [3].

#### 2.3 DeformableTST (NeurIPS 2024)

The NeurIPS 2024 paper "DeformableTST: Transformer for Time Series Forecasting without Over-reliance on Patching" (Donghao Luo and Xue Wang, Tsinghua University) identifies a critical issue: recent Transformer-based time series forecasting models over-rely on the patching technique. Through effective receptive field (ERF) analysis, the authors show that full attention mechanisms cannot focus on important time points by themselves and depend on patching for guidance, limiting applicability to tasks with short input lengths unsuitable for patching. A surprising finding: without patching, nearly all time points in the input series are equally focused by the model and performance worsens (MSE 0.385), exposing "distracted attention." DeformableTST proposes **deformable attention**, a data-driven sparse attention mechanism that samples important time points via learnable offsets, plus a hierarchical structure to mitigate efficiency issues from removing patching. Experiments across long-term forecasting (8 benchmarks with input lengths 96, 384, 768), multivariate short-term forecasting (8 benchmarks), and univariate short-term forecasting (7 benchmarks) show consistent state-of-the-art performance, with averaged 14.1% SMAPE improvement in univariate tasks and averaged 25.6% MSE improvement in multivariate tasks versus the second-best model. Code: https://github.com/luodhhh/DeformableTST [4].

#### 2.4 TimeGPT (Nixtla Foundation Model)

TimeGPT by Nixtla is described as the first foundation model purpose-built for time series forecasting. It uses a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture trained on over 100 billion data points from diverse domains (retail, energy, finance, IoT). Key capabilities include zero-shot inference — generating accurate predictions on unseen datasets without retraining — and probabilistic outputs by default. It is delivered as a low-code, API-driven solution that also supports anomaly detection, performing forecasting in as little as three lines of code [5].

In a Turing Post interview, Nixtla co-founders Azul Garza and Max Mergenthaler explain that TimeGPT is a generative pre-trained transformer but **not an LLM** — it processes time series data (timestamps, values, exogenous variables) rather than text, with no embedding process. It was trained on a proprietary dataset of over 100 billion data points. Key claims: TimeGPT outperforms classical and deep learning models in zero-shot benchmarks across 300,000+ series, especially for weekly and monthly data; it achieves 0.6 ms average GPU inference per series. Nixtla's benchmarks claim LagLlama is 40% less accurate than Seasonal Naive and 1000x slower, Chronos is 10% less accurate and 500% slower than statistical models, and Moirai performs well on hourly data but is up to 33% less accurate on monthly/weekly/yearly data. The model supports uncertainty quantification via conformal prediction and offers covariate weight analysis for what-if scenarios. The co-founders recommend the book "Forecasting: Principles and Practice" and advise: "Learn the basics. Always benchmark. Simpler is many times better. Prophet is a bad forecasting algorithm" [6].

Nixtla positions itself as "to numbers what Anthropic or OpenAI are to language and images." TimeGPT was trained on over 100 billion rows of time series data spanning financial, weather, energy, and web data. Nixtla's open-source ecosystem has more than 5 million downloads worldwide, and its software is used in production by Amazon, Walmart, and Lyft [7].

### 3. Tabular Data Transformers

#### 3.1 FT-Transformer

The FT-Transformer (Feature Tokenizer + Transformer) was introduced in the paper "Revisiting Deep Learning Models for Tabular Data" (Gorishniy et al., 2021, arXiv:2106.11959v2). It builds on the earlier TabTransformer model and addresses its key drawback: numerical features were not used in constructing contextual embeddings. FT-Transformer makes two main changes: (1) it adds linear numerical embeddings — each numeric feature is passed through its own fully connected layer (weights not shared) to produce a dense vector, allowing numerical features to flow through the Transformer blocks alongside categorical embeddings; and (2) it uses a CLS token, appended to the embedded features, which is contextualized by the Transformer and then fed into an MLP for prediction [15][16].

Reported results show FT-Transformer outperforming gradient boosting models and ResNet on various datasets, with low sensitivity to hyperparameters. One validation on the Adult Income Dataset using the `tabtransformertf` package achieved accuracy of 0.8576, close to the reported 0.86. The model provides built-in explainability by deriving feature importances from attention weights (summing CLS attention scores across heads and layers, divided by heads × depth). Top features for income prediction (age, education, marital status, capital gains) aligned with intuition. The article concludes FT-Transformer narrows the gap with gradient-boosted trees while offering explainability [16].

Key components of FT-Transformer: (1) input embeddings converting categorical and numerical features into continuous vector representations; (2) Transformer encoder layers using multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks to capture feature dependencies; (3) feature-wise transformation learning interactions between features in a direct and interpretable way; and (4) an output layer for predictions or classifications. Advantages include interpretable feature interactions, scalability due to parallelization, and strong generalization without extensive feature engineering. Potential applications span financial forecasting, healthcare analytics, and e-commerce personalization [15].

#### 3.2 TabTransformer

The TabTransformer is an attention-based neural network for tabular data that reportedly performs nearly as well as gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT). An update in the `lucidrains/tab-transformer-pytorch` repository notes Amazon AI claims to have beaten GBDT with attention on a real-world tabular dataset (predicting shipping cost). The repository includes both the original TabTransformer and the improved FT-Transformer variant from Yandex (simpler continuous-value embedding scheme). Installation via pip (`tab-transformer-pytorch`), MIT-licensed, 1.1k stars, 132 forks. The README mentions unsupervised training by applying Electra-style pretraining to the transformer module [17].

The TabTransformer architecture consists of column embeddings, transformer layers, and an MLP. It leverages self-attention to generate rich, context-aware embeddings for categorical variables. A comprehensive guide demonstrates training a TabTransformer on the UCI Adult income dataset using Amazon SageMaker with hyperparameter optimization via Optuna and deployment through a Flask-based inference server, using focal loss to handle class imbalance. The guide covers AWS infrastructure (CloudFormation, VPC, RDS, SageMaker, ECR), Hydra configuration, distributed training, and managed spot instances (parameters: max_run, max_wait, max_retry_attempts, use_spot_instances, checkpoint_s3_uri) [18].

### 4. Audio/Speech Transformers (Whisper Fine-Tuning)

#### 4.1 Whisper Model Overview

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model — a Transformer-based encoder-decoder (sequence-to-sequence) model pre-trained on 680,000 hours of labelled audio-transcription data, including 117,000 hours of multilingual data, enabling application to over 96 languages. This is an order of magnitude more data than the unlabelled audio used to train Wav2Vec 2.0 (60,000 hours). Unlike Wav2Vec 2.0, Whisper learns a direct speech-to-text mapping during pre-training, so it requires relatively little fine-tuning [20][21].

#### 4.2 Fine-Tuning Approaches and Results

**Hugging Face guide (multilingual ASR):** Demonstrates fine-tuning the multilingual 'small' checkpoint (244M parameters) on Hindi from the Common Voice 11.0 dataset, using approximately 8 hours of training data and 4 hours of held-out test data. Key steps: loading the WhisperFeatureExtractor (pads/truncates audio to 30 seconds, converts to log-Mel spectrograms at 16kHz), WhisperTokenizer (language='Hindi', task='transcribe'), WhisperProcessor, data collator (padding replaced with -100), WER evaluation, and Seq2SeqTrainingArguments with the Trainer. Training for 5000 steps yielded a best WER of 32.0% after 4000 steps, compared to 63.5% for the pre-trained model — a 31.5% absolute improvement from just 8 hours of training data. Results could be improved with hyperparameter tuning or larger checkpoints ('medium' or 'large-v3') [20].

**Graphcore guide (IPUs):** Fine-tuning Whisper Small on the Catalan subset of OpenSLR (SLR69). The fine-tuning process takes 6–18 minutes on 4 IPUs and achieves a final WER of around 10%. Lists open-source audio datasets for fine-tuning: Common Voice (16,400 hours, 100 languages), Multilingual LibriSpeech (6,000 hours, 7 languages), LibriSpeech (1,000 hours, English), VoxPopuli (1,800 hours, 16 languages), and Fleurs (12 hours per language, 102 languages) [21].

**LearnOpenCV guide (custom ATC dataset):** Fine-tunes Whisper on the atco2-asr-atcosim dataset (8,092 training and 2,026 validation samples) using three smaller Whisper variants — Tiny (39M params), Base (74M), and Small (244M). Training: 10 epochs, batch size 32, learning rate 1e-5, WER as evaluation metric. Whisper Small achieved the best WER of 3.15 at epoch 7, dramatically outperforming the pretrained models, which produced unusable transcriptions on ATC audio. Inference time comparisons on an RTX 3070 Ti showed Tiny is fastest but least accurate, while Small is slowest but most accurate. Notes that fine-tuning ASR models typically requires 20–40 GB of VRAM. Provides a Gradio UI script for interactive inference [22].

**Springer paper (low-resource strategies):** Published June 2024 in the EURASIP Journal on Audio, Speech, and Music Processing. Using Whisper Large-v2 as the pretrained baseline and limited supervised data from seven low-resource languages (Afrikaans, Belarusian, Icelandic, Kazakh, Marathi, Nepali, Swahili) from the FLEURS dataset, evaluated five fine-tuning strategies: vanilla fine-tuning (FT), fine-tuning with frozen encoder bottom layers (FFT), re-initialization fine-tuning (RIFT), bottleneck adapter fine-tuning (BAFT), and LoRA fine-tuning (LoRAFT). Key findings:
- All strategies significantly improved performance over the pretrained model; vanilla FT reduced average WER by 56.94% relative.
- Freezing bottom encoder layers (FFT) further reduced WER by 6.27% relative compared to FT while reducing computational cost; CKA analysis confirmed bottom layers encode language-shared features and top layers encode language-specific features.
- Re-initializing top encoder layers (RIFT) was ineffective and degraded performance.
- Parameter-efficient methods (BAFT and LoRAFT) achieved near-FT performance while updating only ~0.8% and ~0.67% of model parameters respectively, reducing training time by 5.2x and 5.6x, and mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
- Conclusion: freezing bottom layers offers the strongest performance, while adapter-based methods provide the best trade-off for efficiency and generalization [23].

### 5. Graph Transformers

#### 5.1 Motivation: Limitations of Message-Passing GNNs

Message-passing GNNs (GCN uses element-wise mean, GraphSAGE element-wise max, GAT attention-weighted sums) have key limitations: over-squashing (information from distant nodes is compressed and lost — "like being stuck in traffic"), over-smoothing (node embeddings become indistinguishable after many layers — "like being lost in traffic"), limited expressiveness relative to the WL test, and inability to capture long-range dependencies. Graph transformers address these by applying the full transformer architecture — multi-head attention, layer normalization, feed-forward networks, residual connections — to graph nodes, enabling direct modeling of dependencies between any two nodes. A central challenge is encoding graph structure, since standard transformers are structure-agnostic [25][26].

Positional encodings: **Laplacian Positional Encoding (LapPE)** uses the k smallest non-trivial eigenvectors of the normalized graph Laplacian as node positions, generalizing sinusoidal positional encodings from NLP. LapPE is global and distance-aware but suffers from sign ambiguity, often handled by random sign flips during training. **Spectral Attention Networks (SAN)** improve on this with learnable positional encodings (LPE Transformer) and two separate attention mechanisms — one for connected nodes and one for non-connected 'virtual' edges. **SignNet** and **BasisNet** offer sign-invariant architectures: SignNet processes each eigenvector v and -v through shared networks and aggregates results; BasisNet uses outer products v_i v_i^T. A function h is sign-invariant if and only if it can be expressed as h(x) = φ(x) + φ(-x) [25].

Current research frontiers: scalability (vanilla attention is O(N²); approaches include linear attention/Exphormer, graph sparsification, hybrid GPS/GPS++ frameworks), state-space models adapted to graphs (GraphMamba using BFS/DFS traversal), and higher-order topological deep learning. Applications: drug discovery and molecular property prediction, physics simulation, recommender systems, and traffic prediction. A PyG implementation for node classification on the Cora dataset achieves 80% accuracy [25].

#### 5.2 Exphormer (Google Research, ICML 2023)

Exphormer is a sparse attention framework for graph transformers designed to overcome the scalability limitations of standard graph transformers, which typically cannot handle graphs larger than a few thousand nodes due to quadratic computational and memory costs. Exphormer uses expander graphs — sparse yet well-connected graphs with strong spectral properties and rapid random walk mixing — to construct a sparse interaction graph. The framework combines three edge types: edges from the input graph (local attention), edges from a constant-degree expander graph (expander attention), and edges to a small set of virtual nodes (global attention). This results in linear complexity in the number of nodes and edges. The authors prove Exphormer is as expressive as dense transformers and retains universal approximation properties. Built on the GraphGPS framework, Exphormer achieves comparable or better performance than dense attention models, often with fewer parameters, and scales to large graphs including ogbn-arxiv

### 1. SSL Landscape and Method Taxonomy

**Definition and background (IBM):** Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a machine learning technique that uses unsupervised learning for tasks that conventionally require supervised learning. Rather than relying on labeled datasets for supervisory signals, self-supervised models generate implicit labels from unstructured data. Yann LeCun described the process as: "pretend there is a part of the input you don't know and predict that." SSL is technically a subset of unsupervised learning (all SSL techniques are unsupervised, but most unsupervised learning does not entail self-supervision). The term "pretext" implies the training task is not necessarily useful unto itself — it is useful only because it teaches models data representations useful for subsequent downstream tasks. The term is often attributed to Yann LeCun, with conceptual origins in a 2007 paper by Raina et al. [9]

**Two main SSL technique categories (IBM):** (1) **Self-predictive learning** — includes autoencoders, autoregression, masking, and innate relationship prediction; (2) **Contrastive learning** — includes instance discrimination, non-contrastive learning, and multi-modal learning. Notable models: BERT, GPT, LLaMa, Claude, SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, Barlow Twins, and CLIP. Key use cases: NLP (Google's use of BERT in Search, autoregressive LLMs); computer vision where SSL has matched or exceeded supervised performance, including medical imaging (publications grew over 1,000% from 2019 to 2021) and ImageNet accuracy above 80% with only 1% labeled data; image processing/synthesis (denoising autoencoders in Stable Diffusion, PixelCNN, VAEs in DALL-E, CLIP for text-to-image generation). [9]

**Masked modeling survey (arXiv 2401.00897v1, Dec 2023):** Comprehensive review of masked modeling for SSL across vision, language, audio, graph, and biological domains. Proposes a unified framework of four modules: **Mask, Target, Encoder, and Head**, categorizing masked image modeling (MIM) into a taxonomy (BTPM, BTTM, BTFM). Details masking strategies (basic random/AR masking; advanced hard sampling, mixture, adversarial, contextual masking), reconstruction targets (raw pixels, tokenizers, low-level features like HOG/Fourier, high-level features from teachers), architectures (Transformer, hierarchical Transformer, CNN, hybrids), and prediction heads (MIM decoder, contrastive head, or both). Covers applications in video representation, detection/recognition, medical imaging, OCR, remote sensing, low-level vision, 3D point clouds, and other modalities (audio/speech via masked spectrogram modeling, graphs via masked node/edge reconstruction, biology/chemistry via protein and molecule masked modeling). **Theoretical note: MIM captures low-level features with local bias while contrastive learning captures high-level features.** Future directions: efficient MIM design, explainability, multimodal integration. [3]

### 2. Hybrid Contrastive + Masked Modeling (Key Novel-Ingredient Direction)

**CMFM — Contrastive Masked Feature Modeling (Pang et al., Remote Sensing 2026, 18(4), 626):** A self-supervised framework for high-resolution remote sensing image semantic segmentation that addresses limitations of single-strategy SSL (contrastive learning and masked modeling) by combining both in a dual-branch architecture. One branch uses SimCLR-based contrastive learning to capture global feature representations; the other uses masked feature modeling (MFM) for fine-grained local details. Architecture: hybrid CNN+Transformer (ResNet50 feature extractor + 12-layer ViT encoder) with shared-weight encoder, CLR decoder, and lightweight 6-layer MFM decoder. Composite loss balances InfoNCE contrastive loss and L1 reconstruction loss (weights 0.1 and 1.0). Evaluated on WHU Building, Massachusetts Buildings, and GID-5 datasets. Results: on WHU at 5% training data, CMFM achieves 82.70% IoU (16.47% improvement over BEiT); at 100% data, 87.94% IoU. Outperforms BEiT, SimMIM, MAE, CAE, MFM, data2vec. **Key finding: the fusion advantage of dual branches diminishes as dataset scale increases — 2.63% improvement over CLR alone at 5% sample size, but only 0.77% at 100%.** Ablations confirm effectiveness of dual-branch design, random mask ratios (25–80%), 6-layer decoder depth, and CNN+Transformer hybrid. Limitations: validated only on datasets with well-defined object boundaries. [1]

**AC-MAE — Adaptive Contrastive Masked Autoencoding (Stanford CS231N 2025 paper, Karan Singh):** Extends Masked Autoencoders (MAE) for structured representation learning by combining standard MAE reconstruction with a **supervised contrastive loss applied to visible patch tokens**, using coarse labels (superclasses or demographic attributes) during pretraining. A ramp-up schedule delays and gradually increases the contrastive weight to avoid early training collapse. Built on CrossMAE architecture; evaluated on CIFAR-100 and resting-state fMRI data from HCP-YA. Results: on CIFAR-100, up to 12.2% top-1 accuracy improvement in low-data regimes (27.39% → 39.62% at 1% training data), diminishing gains as data increases, slight drop at full data (82.83% vs. 83.81% baseline). On fMRI: 96.83% balanced accuracy and 97.14% F1 for binary sex classification via linear probing vs. 59.13%/61.55% baseline. Learned embeddings show improved semantic clustering (higher silhouette scores). Conclusion: injecting coarse supervision during masked autoencoding improves sample efficiency and representation structure, particularly in data-limited settings. [2]

**TimeMAE (arXiv 2303.00320v4):** Self-supervised framework for time series classification addressing limitations of point-level, unidirectional masked modeling. Two innovations: (1) **semantic unit elevation** — time series segmented into non-overlapping sub-series via window slicing for semantically richer units and reduced compute; (2) **decoupled representation learning** — a decoupled masked autoencoder separately encodes visible and masked regions to avoid artificial masked tokens in the main encoder and reduce pretraining/fine-tuning discrepancy. Pre-training uses two complementary objectives: **masked codeword classification (MCC)** (discretizes sub-series semantics via a learned tokenizer with a codebook) and **masked representation regression (MRR)** (aligns continuous representations using a momentum-updated target encoder). Evaluated on five public datasets: **HAR, PS, AD, Uwave, Epilepsy**. Outperforms TST, TNC, TS-TCC, TS2Vec, SimMTM, FineZero, FineZero+ in one-to-one and one-to-many transfer, label-scarce scenarios, and larger model sizes. Key results: 91.31% accuracy (FineLast) on HAR vs. 87.82% for best baseline TNC; 99.35% accuracy (FineAll) on Epilepsy vs. 97.83% for SimMTM. **A simple random masking strategy with a relatively high masking ratio of 60% yields effective representations.** Code: https://github.com/Mingyue-Cheng/TimeMAE [17]

**DropPatch (AAAI-25):** Strategy to enhance masked time-series modeling by randomly dropping sub-sequence-level patches before masking and reconstruction. Built on PatchTST backbone. Addresses a dilemma: low mask ratios lead to superficial learning/over-fitting (periodic patterns recoverable without high-level understanding); excessively high mask ratios cause scattered attention and degraded representations. Defaults: drop ratio 0.6, mask ratio 0.4. Dropped patches are entirely excluded from training; masked patches remain as zero tensors with positional encoding. Advantages: (1) improved pre-training efficiency with square-level computational gains; (2) performance improvements across in-domain, cross-domain, few-shot (100/300/500 samples), and cold-start (lookback 96) settings. **Theoretical proof: DropPatch slows the rate at which Transformer representations collapse into a rank-1 linear subspace.** Experiments on 12 datasets (Weather, ECL, Traffic, 4 ETT datasets, Exchange, PEMS) — surpasses PatchTST, SimMTM, Ti-MAE, TST, LaST, CoST, TS2Vec, iTransformer, DLinear, FEDformer in 13 of 14 in-domain metrics. Authors compiled two synthesized multi-dataset corpora: **STS66M (3.76M data points) and STS162M (32.5M data points)** for time-series foundation models. Efficiency example on ETTm1: 1404MB/32.2s per epoch vs. PatchTST's 1722MB/44.5s and SimMTM's 29090MB/823.3s. Four empirical findings: (1) DropPatch enables attention heads to capture multi-scale info; (2) sharpens attention head focus (higher KL divergence from uniform); (3) reduces redundancy (higher KL divergence between heads in same layer); (4) CKA analysis shows improved representation ability — higher CKA for in-domain, lower for cross-domain. Applied only during pre-training. [20]

**VisionTS (ICML 2025 poster):** Time series forecasting (TSF) foundation model built from **visual masked autoencoders pre-trained on ImageNet**. Reformulates TSF as an image reconstruction task, bridging image pre-training and TSF. Achieves better zero-shot forecasting than existing TSF foundation models **without any adaptation to time series data**; with just one epoch of fine-tuning, attains SOTA in most cases. Authors highlight intrinsic similarities between images and real-world time series — "free lunch" for TSF, opening cross-modality research directions. Code publicly available on GitHub. [16]

**Forecast-MAE (arXiv 2308.09882, HKUST Guangzhou):** Self-supervised pre-training for motion forecasting extending MAE. Treats motion forecasting as scene reconstruction — reconstructs masked agent trajectories and lane segments. **Core innovation: complementary masking strategy — for each agent, either the entire history or entire future trajectory is masked (never both); lane segments randomly masked.** Asymmetric encoder-decoder with standard Transformer blocks; agent trajectories embedded via FPN with 1D neighborhood attention, lane segments via Mini-PointNet. Pre-training loss: L1 for trajectory reconstruction + MSE for lane reconstruction. Fine-tuning removes decoder/mask tokens and future trajectory inputs, adds multi-modal prediction heads (Huber loss + cross-entropy confidence loss, winner-take-all). On **Argoverse 2 benchmark**: competitive with SOTA supervised methods; outperforms prior SSL method (SSL-Lanes) significantly; superior cross-city generalization. Ensemble improves minFDE₁ by 7.5% over second-best. Code: github.com/jchengai/forecast-mae [18]

**TRACE (GitHub, anonymousgit234):** "Time Series Representation Learning with Contrastive Embeddings for Anomaly Detection in Photovoltaic Systems" — combines self-supervised contrastive learning with autoencoder-based augmentations for time series anomaly detection (TSAD). Evaluated on open-source datasets **SWAT and SMD**, plus a real-world Photovoltaic Inverters Dataset (PID). Two augmentation categories: classical time-series perturbations (warping, masking, permuting, scaling, slicing, time-shifting, freq-shifting, jittering) and autoencoder-based augmentations (CNN-AE, CNN-ATTN-AE, LSTM-AE, LSTM-ATTN-AE, Masked-BiLSTM-ATTN-AE, MultiHead-LSTM-ATTN-AE, Transformer-AE). **TransformerAE backbone achieves superior performance (21.3% F1 improvement) and is the primary backbone.** [32]

### 4. Tabular SSL (Non-Image Modality — Feasible First Project Direction)

**Masked Contrastive Learning (MCL) / AMCL (Hugh Bishop, MPhil dissertation, University of Cambridge, Sept 2021):** Novel approaches to SSL for tabular data. Notes most contrastive methods rely on domain-specific augmentations (e.g., for images) unsuitable for tabular data. **MCL generates positive pairs by randomly masking input features with a Bernoulli distribution and uses InfoNCE loss — requires no strong inductive biases about data structure.** Benchmarked against supervised baselines (logistic regression, XGBoost, MLP), self-supervised methods (DAE, VIME), and naive contrastive approaches (Noise CL, CutMix CL) on Tabular MNIST (classification), UCI Income (classification), UCI Wine Quality (regression). With only 500 labeled instances, MCL achieves best performance on all three (89.6% accuracy on MNIST, 88.4% on UCI Income, MAE 0.0782 on Wine Quality). Findings: independent masking outperforms complementary masking; masking at input layer superior to masking at hidden layer. **AMCL (extension)** learns a correlated masking distribution using hierarchical reparameterisation trick with Concrete/Gumbel-Sigmoid distribution — learns to avoid masking correlated informative features simultaneously. Improves UCI Income and Wine Quality, no change on MNIST. Conclusion: contrastive learning can be successfully applied to tabular data without inductive biases, achieving SOTA self-supervised results. [11]

**STab (NeurIPS 2022 Table Representation Learning Workshop, Hajiramezanali et al.):** Addresses the difficulty of SSL for tabular data, which lacks spatial/semantic structure, making traditional augmentations (rotation, token masking, edge dropping) ineffective. **STab is an augmentation-free self-supervised representation learning method based on stochastic regularization techniques that does not rely on negative pairs.** Achieves SOTA performance compared to existing contrastive and pretext-task SSL methods. [12]

**Attention vs. Contrastive Learning of Tabular Data — data-centric benchmarking (arXiv 2401.04266v1, published Aug 24, 2026; supported by AFOSR Grant W911NF-23-1-0170):** Evaluates 13 methods across four categories — traditional ML (Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting Trees), traditional deep learning (DNN, DNN-AE), attention-based (TabNet, FT-Transformer, NPT, SAINT), and contrastive learning (SCARF with five corruption strategies plus proposed WCR method) — on 28 tabular datasets (14 easy, 14 hard) using weighted F1, average ranks, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Key findings: (1) Among contrastive methods, **CutMix and Random Feature Corruption perform best**, but no corruption (Pass) is competitive on easy datasets; (2) Attention-based methods, especially **SAINT (combines attention and contrastive learning), significantly outperform traditional ML on hard datasets** (SAINT average rank 1.69 vs. GBT 5.79), while traditional methods remain competitive on easy datasets; (3) Attention methods fail with out-of-memory errors on high-dimensional data (500+ features), where contrastive learning takes a robust lead; (4) GBT excels on low feature-sample ratio datasets but declines on high-dimensional ones; (5) DNN-AE is the best traditional deep learning method on easy datasets. Conclusion: dataset structure and statistics should guide model selection; hybrid attention-contrastive approaches like SAINT offer the best performance trade-off. [13]

**Sebastian Raschka's "Deep Learning for Tabular Data" chronology (Jul 24, 2022; updated Jan 23, 2023) — important caveats:** Deep learning is best suited for unstructured data; tabular data usually consists of already-extracted features, so conventional ML is generally recommended as baselines. Key papers: **GReaT** (Oct 2022) uses pretrained transformer-decoder LLMs (GPT-2, DistilGPT-2) to generate realistic synthetic tabular data; **TabPFN** (Oct 2022) transformer solving small tabular classification in a single forward pass, no training/hyperparameter tuning; **TabDDPM** (Sep 2022) diffusion model for synthetic tabular data (multinomial diffusion for categorical, Gaussian for continuous), outperformed GAN/VAE/SMOTE methods; **Grinsztajn et al. (Jul 2022)** found tree-based models (random forests, XGBoost) still outperform deep learning on medium-sized tabular datasets (~10k examples), gap narrows at ~50k; uninformative features hurt deep learning more; **GATE** (Jul 2022) gated additive tree ensemble, tied with LightGBM on large datasets; **pretraining objectives study (Jul 2022)** — MLPs with target-aware mask-based pretraining performed best across 11 datasets, beating gradient boosting on most but not all; **transfer learning for tabular (Jun 2022)** — supervised pretraining outperformed self-supervised pretraining; MLPs beat transformers when target data is scarce; **SAINT** (Jun 2021) uses row and column attention with contrastive pretraining, on average outperformed gradient-boosted trees across nine datasets; **VIME** (Jun 2020) self- and semi-supervised framework, best variant outperformed XGBoost on five datasets; **TabNet** (Aug 2019) attention-based architecture, mixed results vs. gradient boosting. **Raschka's recommendation: start with a random forest, then HistGradientBoosting, then XGBoost, and only try deep learning methods if time and curiosity allow.** [14]

**Awesome Self-Supervised Learning for Non-Sequential Tabular Data (SSL4NSTD) GitHub (wwweiwei):** Curated collection; survey "A Survey on Self-Supervised Learning for Non-Sequential Tabular Data" (ACML-24 Journal Track, arXiv:2402.01204). Papers organized into Predictive Learning, Contrastive Learning, Hybrid Learning. **Six major benchmarks:** MLPCBench (Classification, 40 datasets, Kadra et al. 2021); DLBench (Classification and Regression, 11 datasets, Shwartz-Ziv and Armon 2022); TabularBench (Classification and Regression, 45 datasets, Grinsztajn et al. 2022); TabZilla (Classification, 36 datasets, McElfresh et al. 2023); TabPretNet (Unlabeled, Classification, Regression, 2000 datasets, Ye et al. 2023); The Tremendous TabLib Trawl / T4 (Unlabeled, 3.1M datasets, Gardner et al. 2024). Last updated April 2026. [15]

### 5. Audio/Speech SSL (Non-Image Modality — Challenging Direction)

**wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski, Zhou, Mohamed, Auli; NeurIPS 2020, Facebook AI):** Framework for SSL of speech representations from raw audio. Multi-layer convolutional neural network encodes raw audio into latent speech representations; spans of these latent representations are masked (like BERT masked language modeling); a Transformer builds contextualized representations. **Contrastive task: model must identify the true quantized latent speech representation among distractors; discrete speech units learned via Gumbel softmax product quantization.** Pre-trained on unlabeled speech, fine-tuned on labeled data with CTC loss. Key results: 1.8/3.3 WER on Librispeech clean/other using all 960 hours of labeled data; outperforms previous SOTA on the 100-hour subset while using 100x less labeled data; **4.8/8.2 WER with only 10 minutes of labeled data and pre-training on 53k hours of unlabeled data** (LARGE model, 317M parameters, pre-trained on LibriVox 53.2k hours). New SOTA on TIMIT phoneme recognition (7.4/8.3 PER). Ablations: continuous inputs with quantized targets perform best (quantizing inputs loses information; continuous targets make the task too easy by capturing speaker/background artifacts).
